recommended.name: Resisted Quadriceps Test
recommended.procedure: Patient seated with knee slightly flexed. Examiner applies resistance as the patient extends the knee. If positive, indicates patellofemoral joint irritation.

recommended.name: Step-Down Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands on a 20 cm step and slowly lowers the contralateral heel to the ground while examiner observes knee alignment. If positive, suggests PFPS and poor lower limb control.

recommended.name: Clarke's Test (Patellar Grind Test)
recommended.procedure: Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner applies gentle downward pressure on the superior pole of the patella while patient contracts the quadriceps. If positive, indicates patellofemoral joint dysfunction.

recommended.name: Patellar Apprehension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine and relaxed. Examiner gently pushes the patella laterally. If positive, indicates patellar instability.

recommended.name: Patellar Tilt Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner lifts the lateral edge of the patella while stabilizing the medial edge. If positive, limited tilt or pain indicates tight lateral structures or OA changes.

recommended.name: Waldron Test
recommended.procedure: Patient seated and actively flexes and extends the knee while examiner palpates the patellofemoral joint. If positive, indicates PFPS or patellofemoral joint irritation.

recommended.name: Patellar Glide Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner glides the patella medially and laterally. If positive, indicates abnormal patellar tracking.

questions.questionText: Was there a twisting injury to the knee?

recommended.name: McMurray Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine. Examiner flexes the hip and knee fully, then rotates the tibia internally and externally while extending the knee. If positive, suggests meniscal tear.

recommended.name: Apley's Compression Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies prone with knee flexed to 90°. Examiner applies downward pressure along the tibia while rotating it internally and externally. If positive, indicates meniscal injury.

recommended.name: Thessaly Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands on one leg with knee slightly flexed (~20°). Patient rotates the body and knee internally and externally three times. If positive, indicates possible meniscal pathology.

recommended.name: Bounce Home Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine. Examiner fully flexes the knee and then allows it to passively extend. If positive, suggests a displaced meniscal fragment.

recommended.name: Ege's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands with knees flexed and externally rotates both feet to test the medial meniscus; internally rotates both feet to test the lateral meniscus. If positive, pain or clicking occurs along the joint line.

questions.questionText: Is the pain aggravated by stretching or contracting the muscle?

recommended.name: Resisted Contraction Test
recommended.procedure: Patient contracts the affected muscle against resistance at mid-range. Positive if pain is reproduced at the site.

recommended.name: Passive Stretch Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner stretches the affected muscle slowly. Positive if pain is reproduced.

recommended.name: Lachman Test
recommended.procedure: Knee flexed ~30°, examiner stabilizes femur and pulls tibia anteriorly at the knee. Positive sign = soft endpoint or increased anterior tibial translation indicates ACL tear.

recommended.name: Anterior Drawer Test
recommended.procedure: Knee flexed 90°, examiner pulls tibia anteriorly at the knee. Positive sign = increased anterior translation indicates ACL injury.

questions.questionText: Was there a direct blow to the OUTSIDE of the knee (pushing it inward)?

recommended.name: Valgus Stress Test
recommended.procedure: With pt supine, knee flexed to 30°, examiner stabilizes the femur and applies a valgus force to the knee. Positive sign = pain or gapping at the medial knee joint line indicates MCL injury.

questions.questionText: Was there a direct blow to the INSIDE of the knee (pushing it outward)?
Is the pain and tenderness on the OUTER (lateral) side of the knee?

recommended.name: Varus Stress Test
recommended.procedure: With pt supine, knee flexed to 30°, examiner stabilizes the femur and applies a varus force to the knee. Positive sign = pain or gapping at the lateral knee joint line indicates LCL injury.

questions.questionText: Was the injury a blow to the front of the bent knee, or a hyperextension?

recommended.name: Posterior Drawer Test
recommended.procedure: Knee flexed 90°, examiner pushes tibia posteriorly at the knee. Positive sign = posterior translation indicates PCL tear.

recommended.name: Godfrey (Posterior Sag) Test
recommended.procedure: Hip and knee flexed 90°, examiner observes tibial plateau at the knee. Positive sign = sagging tibia compared to contralateral knee indicates PCL injury.

recommended.name: Patellofemoral Compression Test (Grind Test)
recommended.procedure: Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner applies downward pressure on the patella while asking the patient to contract the quadriceps. Positive sign = pain or crepitus at the patellofemoral joint.

recommended.name: Patellar Tilt Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner lifts the lateral edge of the patella while stabilizing the medial edge. Positive sign = limited tilt or pain indicates tight lateral structures or OA changes.

recommended.name: Crepitus Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner moves the knee through full flexion and extension, palpating and listening for audible or palpable crepitus.

recommended.name: Patellar Apprehension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with the knee extended. Examiner gently pushes the patella laterally. Positive sign = apprehension or pain indicating abnormal patellar tracking.

recommended.name: Patellar Hyper-mobility Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine, knee extended. Examiner gently displaces patella medially and laterally. Positive sign = excessive hypermobility or abnormal motion.

recommended.name: Imaging

recommended.name: Straight Leg Raise Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with both legs extended. Examiner asks the patient to lift the affected leg straight up without bending the knee. Positive sign = inability to lift the leg actively, indicating disruption of the extensor mechanism.

recommended.name: Palpation Test for Patella Integrity
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with knee relaxed. Examiner palpates the patella gently using fingers to feel for tenderness, irregularity, or gap. Positive sign = localized severe tenderness, palpable gap, or irregularity.

recommended.name: Active Knee Extension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient sits or lies supine. Examiner asks patient to actively straighten the knee from a flexed position. Positive sign = inability or severe pain during active extension.

recommended.name: Patellar Compression Test (Modified for fracture screening)
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with knee extended. Examiner gently presses patella posteriorly toward femur. Positive sign = severe localized pain, suggesting patella fracture.

recommended.name: Radiographic Confirmation

recommended.name: Ober's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies on unaffected side. Examiner extends and abducts the hip, then slowly lowers the leg. Positive sign = leg remains elevated and does not drop.

recommended.name: Renne Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands and performs squat while examiner applies pressure over lateral femoral epicondyle. Positive sign = pain at approximately 30° knee flexion.

recommended.name: Modified Thomas Test

recommended.name: Palpation Test of Lateral Femoral Epicondyle

recommended.name: Lateral Lumbar Flexion (Fingertip to Floor Test)
recommended.procedure: The patient stands with heel touching wall and feet wide apart, and back against the wall. Then the examiner measures the distance from middle finger to the floor. Then patient bends to side (lateral flexion). The distance between the middle finger and the floor is measured again. This measurement is done for both sides.

recommended.name: Modified Schober's Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner marks both posterior superior iliac spine, and a horizontal line is drawn between both marks. A second line is marked 5cm below the first line, and a third line is marked 10cm above the first line. Patient is then instructed to flex forward as if attempting to touch their toes. An increase of less than 5cm shows decreased lumbar spine range of motion, and ankylosing spondylitis.

recommended.name: Spurling's Test (for Cervical Radiculitis)
recommended.procedure: While patient is seated, the examiner applies side flexion of the neck towards the affected side while applying axial compression. Sign is positive if the pain sensation felt in the shoulder-neck region is replicated.

recommended.name: Painful Arc Test
recommended.procedure: Ask patient to abduct arm across range of motion actively. Scapular rhythm is disturbed, pain is aggravated between 60-120 degrees, pain is alleviated if shoulder is laterally rotated on abduction. If positive, SIS is indicated.

recommended.name: Neer Impingement Sign
recommended.procedure: Stabilise the scapula with one hand and raise the unaffected side to full flexion with abduction and internal rotation passively. The test is positive when there is pain at the subacromial space.

recommended.name: Hawkins-Kennedy Test
recommended.procedure: Patient arm is placed in 90 deg of elevation at the scapular level and 90 deg flexion. Stabilise the upper arm with one hand and internally rotate with the other hand. The test is positive when pain is felt in the anterolateral aspect of the shoulder.

recommended.name: Jobe's Test
recommended.procedure: Elevate arm in scapular plane, extend elbow and thumb points towards floor with arm internally rotated. Patient is asked to hold the position with downward pressure from examiner. Positive sign = pain on examiner restriction indicating supraspinatus irritation.

recommended.name: Empty Can Test (Supraspinatus)
recommended.procedure: Patient is asked to abduct up to 90 deg, 30 deg flexion and internal rotation. Examiner stands behind patient and applies downward pressure. Positive sign: affected side is weaker than unaffected side. Positive sign suggests tear in the supraspinatus.

recommended.name: Infraspinatus Test
recommended.procedure: Patient holds arms close to body, elbow is flexed up to 90 deg of forward elevation in scapular plane. External rotation is instructed while examiner applies resistance. Lack of power on one side indicates weakness of the infraspinatus muscle.

recommended.name: Subscapularis Test (Belly Press Test)
recommended.procedure: Patient is asked to place their hand on their abdomen and move elbow forward. Patient is then asked to press hand on the abdomen. If subscapularis is torn, patient will be unable to perform movement and elbow will move backwards.

recommended.name: Lag Sign for External Rotation
recommended.procedure: Patient lifts arm slightly from body and is asked to hold in external rotation. Positive when hand recoils to neutral position and suggests tear of infraspinatus or supraspinatus.

recommended.name: Drop Sign
recommended.procedure: The examiner places the arm at 90 deg abduction, elbow at right angle and arm maximally rotated. Positive sign: arm drops from position. Suggests a tear of the infraspinatus or the posterior part of the rotator cuff.

recommended.name: Lift-Off Test (Subscapularis)
recommended.procedure: Patient is asked to place hand on the back at the mid-lumbar spine. The clinician then lifts hand from the back and patient is asked to hold it there. Positive sign: inability to maintain hand while removed suggests subscapularis weakness.

recommended.name: Talar Tilt Test
recommended.procedure: The ankle is held in the neutral position, examiner stabilises the tibia just above the ankle and then tries to force the ankle into maximum inversion. The ROM can be measured or compared with the contralateral side. Inversion laxity suggests injury to calcaneofibular and anterior talofibular ligaments (ATFL).

recommended.name: Anterior Drawer Test
recommended.procedure: Patient sits with knee flexed at 90 deg and ankle in plantarflexion of about 10 deg. The lower leg is stabilised by the examiner and forces patient's heel forward over the tibia. If positive, the talus can be felt sliding forwards and backwards. Laxity indicates tear of the ATFL.

questionResponseTests.question: Where is your pain worse?

recommended.name: Spurling's Test (Maximal Cervical Compression and Foraminal Compression Test)
recommended.procedure: The neck is placed in extension, lateral flexion, and axial compression. The test is positive if pain is present and radiates to the arm.

recommended.name: Cervical Distraction Test
recommended.procedure: The patient lies supine and the neck is positioned comfortably. The examiner places hand around the patient's mastoid process. The examiner then slightly flexes the patient's neck and pulls the head towards your torso. Test is positive if the symptoms reduce or are eliminated with traction.

recommended.name: MRI
recommended.procedure: Radiographic confirmation of disc herniation

recommended.procedure: Check if cervical rotation on the affected side is less than 60 degrees

recommended.name: Single-Leg Stance Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands on the affected leg. Positive sign = pain over the greater trochanter.

recommended.name: Resisted External Derotation Test
recommended.procedure: Patient resists external rotation of the hip. Positive sign = pain at the greater trochanteric region.

recommended.name: Ober's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies on unaffected side. Examiner extends and abducts the hip, then slowly lowers the leg. Positive sign = leg remains elevated and does not drop.

recommended.name: Trendelenburg Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands on one leg. Positive sign = pelvis drops on the contralateral side, indicating gluteal weakness.

questionResponseTests.question: Is the pain worse when descending stairs than ascending?

recommended.name: Resisted Quadriceps Test
recommended.procedure: Patient seated with knee slightly flexed. Examiner applies resistance as the patient extends the knee. If positive, indicates patellofemoral joint irritation.

recommended.name: Step-Down Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands on a 20 cm step and slowly lowers the contralateral heel to the ground while examiner observes knee alignment. If positive, suggests PFPS and poor lower limb control.

recommended.name: Clarke's Test (Patellar Grind Test)
recommended.procedure: Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner applies gentle downward pressure on the superior pole of the patella while patient contracts the quadriceps. If positive, indicates patellofemoral joint dysfunction.

recommended.name: Patellar Apprehension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine and relaxed. Examiner gently pushes the patella laterally. If positive, indicates patellar instability.

recommended.name: Patellar Tilt Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner lifts the lateral edge of the patella while stabilizing the medial edge. If positive, limited tilt or pain indicates tight lateral structures or OA changes.

recommended.name: Waldron Test
recommended.procedure: Patient seated and actively flexes and extends the knee while examiner palpates the patellofemoral joint. If positive, indicates PFPS or patellofemoral joint irritation.

recommended.name: Patellar Glide Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner glides the patella medially and laterally. If positive, indicates abnormal patellar tracking.

recommended.name: Resisted Quadriceps Test
recommended.procedure: Patient seated with knee slightly flexed. Examiner applies resistance as the patient extends the knee. If positive, indicates patellofemoral joint irritation.

recommended.name: Step-Down Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands on a 20 cm step and slowly lowers the contralateral heel to the ground while examiner observes knee alignment. If positive, suggests PFPS and poor lower limb control.

recommended.name: Clarke's Test (Patellar Grind Test)
recommended.procedure: Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner applies gentle downward pressure on the superior pole of the patella while patient contracts the quadriceps. If positive, indicates patellofemoral joint dysfunction.

recommended.name: Patellar Apprehension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine and relaxed. Examiner gently pushes the patella laterally. If positive, indicates patellar instability.

recommended.name: Patellar Tilt Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner lifts the lateral edge of the patella while stabilizing the medial edge. If positive, limited tilt or pain indicates tight lateral structures or OA changes.

recommended.name: Waldron Test
recommended.procedure: Patient seated and actively flexes and extends the knee while examiner palpates the patellofemoral joint. If positive, indicates PFPS or patellofemoral joint irritation.

recommended.name: Patellar Glide Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner glides the patella medially and laterally. If positive, indicates abnormal patellar tracking.

questionResponseTests.question: Was there a twisting injury to the knee?

recommended.name: McMurray Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine. Examiner flexes the hip and knee fully, then rotates the tibia internally and externally while extending the knee. If positive, suggests meniscal tear.

recommended.name: Apley's Compression Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies prone with knee flexed to 90°. Examiner applies downward pressure along the tibia while rotating it internally and externally. If positive, indicates meniscal injury.

recommended.name: Thessaly Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands on one leg with knee slightly flexed (~20°). Patient rotates the body and knee internally and externally three times. If positive, indicates possible meniscal pathology.

recommended.name: Bounce Home Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine. Examiner fully flexes the knee and then allows it to passively extend. If positive, suggests a displaced meniscal fragment.

recommended.name: Ege's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands with knees flexed and externally rotates both feet to test the medial meniscus; internally rotates both feet to test the lateral meniscus. If positive, pain or clicking occurs along the joint line.

recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with the knee extended. Examiner gently pushes the patella laterally. Positive sign = apprehension or pain indicating abnormal patellar tracking.

recommended.name: Patellar Hyper-mobility Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine, knee extended. Examiner gently displaces patella medially and laterally. Positive sign = excessive hypermobility or abnormal motion.

recommended.name: Imaging
recommended.procedure: Lateral and axial X-rays; MRI if soft tissue assessment needed. Positive sign = subluxation/dislocation, osteochondral fractures, or MPFL tear.

questionResponseTests.question: Are you unable to bear weight on the leg since the injury?

effects.redFlagText: Inability to bear weight after trauma — strong fracture indicator; urgent X-ray.

recommended.name: Straight Leg Raise Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with both legs extended. Examiner asks the patient to lift the affected leg straight up without bending the knee. Positive sign = inability to lift the leg actively, indicating disruption of the extensor mechanism.

recommended.name: Palpation Test for Patella Integrity
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with knee relaxed. Examiner palpates the patella gently using fingers to feel for tenderness, irregularity, or gap. Positive sign = localized severe tenderness, palpable gap, or irregularity.

recommended.name: Active Knee Extension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient sits or lies supine. Examiner asks patient to actively straighten the knee from a flexed position. Positive sign = inability or severe pain during active extension.

recommended.name: Patellar Compression Test (Modified for fracture screening)
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with knee extended. Examiner gently presses patella posteriorly toward femur. Positive sign = severe localized pain, suggesting patella fracture.

recommended.name: Radiographic Confirmation
recommended.procedure: Imaging (X-ray – AP, Lateral, Skyline view). Positive sign = visible fracture line, displacement, or comminution.

questionResponseTests.question: Does your activity involve repetitive knee bending (running, cycling)?

recommended.name: Noble Compression Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine. Examiner flexes knee to 90° and applies pressure over lateral femoral epicondyle while slowly extending the knee. Positive sign = pain at approximately 30° knee flexion.

recommended.name: Ober's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies on unaffected side. Examiner extends and abducts the hip, then slowly lowers the leg. Positive sign = leg remains elevated and does not drop.

recommended.name: Renne Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands and performs squat while examiner applies pressure over lateral femoral epicondyle. Positive sign = pain at approximately 30° knee flexion.

recommended.name: Modified Thomas Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine at edge of table. Examiner observes hip and thigh position. Positive sign = tight lateral thigh indicating IT band tightness.

recommended.name: Palpation Test of Lateral Femoral Epicondyle
recommended.procedure: Examiner palpates lateral femoral epicondyle with knee flexed and extended.

recommended.name: Bicycle Stress Test
recommended.procedure: Record the amount of time the patient spends on a cycle ergometer while in a neutral lumbar position and slumped position. If patient spends more time in the slumped position, a lumbar spinal stenosis is indicated.

recommended.name: Two-stage Treadmill Test
recommended.procedure: The patient walks on a flat treadmill and the amount of time spent is recorded and compared with the amount of time while the treadmill is inclined such that patient walks in flexion.

recommended.name: Lumbar Extension-Loading Test
recommended.procedure: The examiner ensures that the lumbar region is in moderate extension (10-30 deg) while standing and patient lies supine. Check if there are changes in the symptoms that the patient feels.

entryCriteria.description: Age (common in teens and early adults)

recommended.name: Lateral Lumbar Flexion (Fingertip to Floor Test)
recommended.procedure: The patient stands with heel touching wall and feet wide apart, and back against the wall. Then the examiner measures the distance from middle finger to the floor. Then patient bends to side (lateral flexion). The distance between the middle finger and the floor is measured again. This measurement is done for both sides.

recommended.name: Modified Schober's Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner marks both posterior superior iliac spine, and a horizontal line is drawn between both marks. A second line is marked 5cm below the first line, and a third line is marked 10cm above the first line. Patient is then instructed to flex forward as if attempting to touch their toes. An increase of less than 5cm shows decreased lumbar spine range of motion, and ankylosing spondylitis.

recommended.name: Chest Expansion Test
recommended.procedure: Normal chest expansion is ≥ 5 cm

recommended.name: Occiput to Wall Distance
recommended.procedure: Normal distance is 0

recommended.name: Tragus to Wall Distance
recommended.procedure: Normal distance is < 15cm

recommended.name: Intermalleolar Distance
recommended.procedure: Normal distance is > 100cm

recommended.name: Laboratory Investigations
recommended.procedure: Confirmatory test through laboratory investigations (HLA-B27, ESR, CRP)

recommended.name: Spurling's Test (for Cervical Radiculitis)
recommended.procedure: While patient is seated, the examiner applies side flexion of the neck towards the affected side while applying axial compression. Sign is positive if the pain sensation felt in the shoulder-neck region is replicated.

recommended.name: Painful Arc Test
recommended.procedure: Ask patient to abduct arm across range of motion actively. Scapular rhythm is disturbed, pain is aggravated between 60-120 degrees, pain is alleviated if shoulder is laterally rotated on abduction. If positive, SIS is indicated.

recommended.name: Neer Impingement Sign
recommended.procedure: Stabilise the scapula with one hand and raise the unaffected side to full flexion with abduction and internal rotation passively. The test is positive when there is pain at the subacromial space.

recommended.name: Hawkins-Kennedy Test
recommended.procedure: Patient arm is placed in 90 deg of elevation at the scapular level and 90 deg flexion. Stabilise the upper arm with one hand and internally rotate with the other hand. The test is positive when pain is felt in the anterolateral aspect of the shoulder.

recommended.name: Jobe's Test
recommended.procedure: Elevate arm in scapular plane, extend elbow and thumb points towards floor with arm internally rotated. Patient is asked to hold the position with downward pressure from examiner. Positive sign = pain on examiner restriction indicating supraspinatus irritation.

questionResponseTests.question: Are you above 45yrs of age?

recommended.name: Empty Can Test (Supraspinatus)
recommended.procedure: Patient is asked to abduct up to 90 deg, 30 deg flexion and internal rotation. Examiner stands behind patient and applies downward pressure. Positive sign: affected side is weaker than unaffected side. Positive sign suggests tear in the supraspinatus.

recommended.name: Infraspinatus Test
recommended.procedure: Patient holds arms close to body, elbow is flexed up to 90 deg of forward elevation in scapular plane. External rotation is instructed while examiner applies resistance. Lack of power on one side indicates weakness of the infraspinatus muscle.

recommended.name: Subscapularis Test (Belly Press Test)
recommended.procedure: Patient is asked to place their hand on their abdomen and move elbow forward. Patient is then asked to press hand on the abdomen. If subscapularis is torn, patient will be unable to perform movement and elbow will move backwards.

recommended.name: Lag Sign for External Rotation
recommended.procedure: Patient lifts arm slightly from body and is asked to hold in external rotation. Positive when hand recoils to neutral position and suggests tear of infraspinatus or supraspinatus.

recommended.name: Drop Sign
recommended.procedure: The examiner places the arm at 90 deg abduction, elbow at right angle and arm maximally rotated. Positive sign: arm drops from position. Suggests a tear of the infraspinatus or the posterior part of the rotator cuff.

recommended.name: Lift-Off Test (Subscapularis)
recommended.procedure: Patient is asked to place hand on the back at the mid-lumbar spine. The clinician then lifts hand from the back and patient is asked to hold it there. Positive sign: inability to maintain hand while removed suggests subscapularis weakness.

questionResponseTests.question: Have you had a previous history of a shoulder dislocation?

recommended.name: Apprehension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient is in sitting or lying position, the examiner lifts the arm gently into abduction, external rotation and then extension. Test is positive if patient senses that humeral head is about to slip out anteriorly and body stiffens in apprehension. The test is repeated with the anterior part of shoulder protected.

recommended.name: Fulcrum's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine, arm abducted up to 90 deg. The examiner places their hands over the shoulder to set the fulcrum base. The humeral head is levered forward by extending and externally rotating arm. The patient immediately becomes apprehensive.

recommended.name: Drawer's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine, scapula is stabilised with one hand while the upper arm is grasped firmly with the other, and manoeuvring is done forward and backward (like a drawer). The drawer's test is positive if instability is marked.

recommended.name: Fulcrum's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine, arm abducted up to 90 deg. The examiner places their hands over the shoulder to set the fulcrum base. The humeral head is levered forward by extending and externally rotating arm. The patient immediately becomes apprehensive.

recommended.name: Drawer's Test

recommended.procedure: The ankle is held in the neutral position, examiner stabilises the tibia just above the ankle and then tries to force the ankle into maximum inversion. recommended.procedure: Patient sits with knee flexed at 90 deg and ankle in plantarflexion of about 10 deg. recommended.name: Trendelenburg Test

recommended.name: Log Roll Test

recommended.name: Thomas Test (Modified)

recommended.procedure: Patient actively moves the hip through flexion/extension and rotation. Positive sign = palpable/audible snap over the hip.

recommended.name: Ober's Test (External Snapping)
recommended.procedure: Patient side-lying, hip abducted and extended, then lowered. Positive sign = snap over greater trochanter in IT band type.

recommended.name: Thomas Test (Internal Snapping)
recommended.procedure: Patient supine, hip flexed to chest, then extended. Positive sign = snap over iliopsoas tendon during extension.

recommended.name: Passive Joint Motion Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner gently moves the knee through passive flexion and extension. Severe pain with passive movement is positive.

recommended.name: Joint Effusion Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner strokes medial and lateral knee. Significant fluid accumulation suggests infection.

recommended.name: Blood Tests
recommended.procedure: Elevated ESR, CRP, WBC count; identifies causative organism

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Is the pain worse when descending stairs than ascending?

recommended.name: Resisted Quadriceps Test
recommended.procedure: Patient seated with knee slightly flexed. Examiner applies resistance as the patient extends the knee. If positive, indicates patellofemoral joint irritation.

recommended.name: Step-Down Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands on a 20 cm step and slowly lowers the contralateral heel to the ground while examiner observes knee alignment. If positive, suggests PFPS and poor lower limb control.

recommended.name: Clarke's Test (Patellar Grind Test)
recommended.procedure: Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner applies gentle downward pressure on the superior pole of the patella while patient contracts the quadriceps. If positive, indicates patellofemoral joint dysfunction.

recommended.name: Patellar Apprehension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine and relaxed. Examiner gently pushes the patella laterally. If positive, indicates patellar instability.

recommended.name: Patellar Tilt Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner lifts the lateral edge of the patella while stabilizing the medial edge. If positive, limited tilt or pain indicates tight lateral structures or OA changes.

recommended.name: Waldron Test
recommended.procedure: Patient seated and actively flexes and extends the knee while examiner palpates the patellofemoral joint. If positive, indicates PFPS or patellofemoral joint irritation.

recommended.name: Patellar Glide Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner glides the patella medially and laterally. If positive, indicates abnormal patellar tracking.

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Was there a twisting injury to the knee?

recommended.name: McMurray Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine. Examiner flexes the hip and knee fully, then rotates the tibia internally and externally while extending the knee. If positive, suggests meniscal tear.

recommended.name: Apley's Compression Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies prone with knee flexed to 90°. Examiner applies downward pressure along the tibia while rotating it internally and externally. If positive, indicates meniscal injury.

recommended.name: Thessaly Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands on one leg with knee slightly flexed (~20°). Patient rotates the body and knee internally and externally three times. If positive, indicates possible meniscal pathology.

recommended.name: Bounce Home Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine. Examiner fully flexes the knee and then allows it to passively extend. If positive, suggests a displaced meniscal fragment.

recommended.name: Ege's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands with knees flexed and externally rotates both feet to test the medial meniscus; internally rotates both feet to test the lateral meniscus. If positive, pain or clicking occurs along the joint line.

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Is the pain aggravated by stretching or contracting the muscle?

recommended.name: Resisted Contraction Test
recommended.procedure: Patient contracts the affected muscle against resistance at mid-range. Positive if pain is reproduced at the site.

recommended.name: Passive Stretch Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner stretches the affected muscle slowly. Positive if pain is reproduced.

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Was the mechanism a non-contact cutting, pivoting, or deceleration move?

recommended.name: Lachman Test
recommended.procedure: Knee flexed ~30°, examiner stabilizes femur and pulls tibia anteriorly at the knee. Positive sign = soft endpoint or increased anterior tibial translation indicates ACL tear.

recommended.name: Anterior Drawer Test
recommended.procedure: Knee flexed 90°, examiner pulls tibia anteriorly at the knee. Positive sign = increased anterior translation indicates ACL injury.

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Was there a direct blow to the OUTSIDE of the knee (pushing it inward)?

recommended.name: Valgus Stress Test
recommended.procedure: With pt supine, knee flexed to 30°, examiner stabilizes the femur and applies a valgus force to the knee. Positive sign = pain or gapping at the medial knee joint line indicates MCL injury.

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Was there a direct blow to the INSIDE of the knee (pushing it outward)?

recommended.name: Varus Stress Test
recommended.procedure: With pt supine, knee flexed to 30°, examiner stabilizes the femur and applies a varus force to the knee. Positive sign = pain or gapping at the lateral knee joint line indicates LCL injury.

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Was the injury a blow to the front of the bent knee, or a hyperextension?

recommended.name: Posterior Drawer Test
recommended.procedure: Knee flexed 90°, examiner pushes tibia posteriorly at the knee. Positive sign = posterior translation indicates PCL tear.

recommended.name: Godfrey (Posterior Sag) Test
recommended.procedure: Hip and knee flexed 90°, examiner observes tibial plateau at the knee. Positive sign = sagging tibia compared to contralateral knee indicates PCL injury.

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Do you have morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes?

recommended.name: Patellofemoral Compression Test (Grind Test)
recommended.procedure: Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner applies downward pressure on the patella while asking the patient to contract the quadriceps. Positive sign = pain or crepitus at the patellofemoral joint.

recommended.name: Patellar Tilt Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner lifts the lateral edge of the patella while stabilizing the medial edge. Positive sign = limited tilt or pain indicates tight lateral structures or OA changes.

recommended.name: Crepitus Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner moves the knee through full flexion and extension, palpating and listening for audible or palpable crepitus.

recommended.name: Radiographic Confirmation
recommended.procedure: Check for joint space narrowing, osteophyte formation, subchondral sclerosis, and cyst formation

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Did you feel the kneecap move out of place?

recommended.name: Patellar Apprehension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with the knee extended. Examiner gently pushes the patella laterally. Positive sign = apprehension or pain indicating abnormal patellar tracking.

recommended.name: Patellar Hyper-mobility Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine, knee extended. Examiner gently displaces patella medially and laterally. Positive sign = excessive hypermobility or abnormal motion.

recommended.name: Imaging
recommended.procedure: Lateral and axial X-rays; MRI if soft tissue assessment needed. Positive sign = subluxation/dislocation, osteochondral fractures, or MPFL tear.

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Are you unable to bear weight on the leg since the injury?

recommended.name: Straight Leg Raise Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with both legs extended. Examiner asks the patient to lift the affected leg straight up without bending the knee. Positive sign = inability to lift the leg actively, indicating disruption of the extensor mechanism.

recommended.name: Palpation Test for Patella Integrity
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with knee relaxed. Examiner palpates the patella gently using fingers to feel for tenderness, irregularity, or gap. Positive sign = localized severe tenderness, palpable gap, or irregularity.

recommended.name: Active Knee Extension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient sits or lies supine. Examiner asks patient to actively straighten the knee from a flexed position. Positive sign = inability or severe pain during active extension.

recommended.name: Patellar Compression Test (Modified for fracture screening)
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with knee extended. Examiner gently presses patella posteriorly toward femur. Positive sign = severe localized pain, suggesting patella fracture.

recommended.name: Radiographic Confirmation
recommended.procedure: Imaging (X-ray – AP, Lateral, Skyline view). Positive sign = visible fracture line, displacement, or comminution.

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Does your activity involve repetitive knee bending (running, cycling)?

recommended.name: Noble Compression Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine. Examiner flexes knee to 90° and applies pressure over lateral femoral epicondyle while slowly extending the knee. Positive sign = pain at approximately 30° knee flexion.

recommended.name: Ober's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies on unaffected side. Examiner extends and abducts the hip, then slowly lowers the leg. Positive sign = leg remains elevated and does not drop.

recommended.name: Renne Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands and performs squat while examiner applies pressure over lateral femoral epicondyle. Positive sign = pain at approximately 30° knee flexion.

recommended.name: Modified Thomas Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine at edge of table. Examiner observes hip and thigh position. Positive sign = tight lateral thigh indicating IT band tightness.

recommended.name: Palpation Test of Lateral Femoral Epicondyle
recommended.procedure: Examiner palpates lateral femoral epicondyle with knee flexed and extended.

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Does your activity involve jumping, sprinting, or frequent knee loading?

recommended.name: Decline Squat Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands on 25° decline board and performs squat. Positive sign = localized pain at inferior pole of patella.

recommended.name: Resisted Knee Extension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient sits with knee flexed. Examiner resists knee extension. Positive sign = localized tendon pain.

recommended.name: Single-Leg Decline Squat Test
recommended.procedure: Patient performs single-leg squat on decline surface. Positive sign = reproduction of localized tendon pain.

recommended.name: Palpation Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner palpates inferior and superior poles of patella. Positive sign = localized tenderness at tendon insertion.

recommended.name: Hop Test
recommended.procedure: Patient performs repeated hopping on affected leg. Positive sign = localized tendon pain with loading.

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Do you have a history of knee osteoarthritis?

recommended.name: Pes Anserinus Palpation Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with knee extended. Examiner palpates 5–7 cm below medial joint line. Positive sign = localized tenderness.

recommended.name: Resisted Knee Flexion Test
recommended.procedure: Patient flexes knee while examiner applies resistance. Positive sign = pain at pes anserinus region.

recommended.name: Resisted Hip Adduction Test
recommended.procedure: Patient performs hip adduction while examiner applies resistance. Positive sign = pain at pes anserinus insertion.

recommended.name: Hamstring Stretch Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner passively stretches hamstrings. Positive sign = pain at pes anserinus region.

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Is there a history of repetitive sports activity (running, jumping, football)?

recommended.name: Wilson's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine. Examiner flexes knee to 90°. Patient actively extends knee while examiner internally rotates tibia. Positive sign = pain between 30°–40° knee extension relieved with external rotation.

recommended.name: Passive Condylar Palpation Test
recommended.procedure: Patient knee flexed to 90°. Examiner palpates femoral condyles. Positive sign = localized pain over femoral condyle.

recommended.name: Joint Effusion Test (Stroke Test)
recommended.procedure: Examiner strokes medial knee upward and lateral knee downward. Positive sign = fluid movement or bulge.

conditionSummary.firstQuestion: Do you notice swelling or a lump behind the knee?

recommended.name: Foucher's Sign

recommended.name: Popliteal Palpation Test

recommended.name: Transillumination Test
recommended.procedure: Light source applied behind swelling. Positive sign = transillumination suggests fluid-filled cyst.

recommended.name: Knee Effusion Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner performs stroke test or bulge test. Positive sign = fluid accumulation present.

recommended.name: Bragard Test
recommended.procedure: This is a modification of the SLR and dorsiflexion is applied at the end of the SLR. This reduces the angle where the test is positive.

recommended.name: Two-stage Treadmill Test
recommended.procedure: The patient walks on a flat treadmill and the amount of time spent is recorded and compared with the amount of time while the treadmill is inclined such that patient walks in flexion.

recommended.name: Lumbar Extension-Loading Test

recommended.name: Lateral Lumbar Flexion (Fingertip to Floor Test)
recommended.procedure: The patient stands with heel touching wall and feet wide apart, and back against the wall. Then the examiner measures the distance from middle finger to the floor. Then patient bends to side (lateral flexion). The distance between the middle finger and the floor is measured again. This measurement is done for both sides.

recommended.name: Modified Schober's Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner marks both posterior superior iliac spine, and a horizontal line is drawn between both marks. A second line is marked 5cm below the first line, and a third line is marked 10cm above the first line. Patient is then instructed to flex forward as if attempting to touch their toes. An increase of less than 5cm shows decreased lumbar spine range of motion, and ankylosing spondylitis.

recommended.name: Spurling's Test (for Cervical Radiculitis)
recommended.procedure: While patient is seated, the examiner applies side flexion of the neck towards the affected side while applying axial compression. Sign is positive if the pain sensation felt in the shoulder-neck region is replicated.

recommended.name: Painful Arc Test
recommended.procedure: Ask patient to abduct arm across range of motion actively. Scapular rhythm is disturbed, pain is aggravated between 60-120 degrees, pain is alleviated if shoulder is laterally rotated on abduction. If positive, SIS is indicated.

recommended.name: Neer Impingement Sign
recommended.procedure: Stabilise the scapula with one hand and raise the unaffected side to full flexion with abduction and internal rotation passively. The test is positive when there is pain at the subacromial space.

recommended.name: Hawkins-Kennedy Test
recommended.procedure: Patient arm is placed in 90 deg of elevation at the scapular level and 90 deg flexion. Stabilise the upper arm with one hand and internally rotate with the other hand. The test is positive when pain is felt in the anterolateral aspect of the shoulder.

recommended.name: Jobe's Test
recommended.procedure: Elevate arm in scapular plane, extend elbow and thumb points towards floor with arm internally rotated. Patient is asked to hold the position with downward pressure from examiner. Positive sign = pain on examiner restriction indicating supraspinatus irritation.

recommended.name: Empty Can Test (Supraspinatus)
recommended.procedure: Patient is asked to abduct up to 90 deg, 30 deg flexion and internal rotation. Examiner stands behind patient and applies downward pressure. Positive sign: affected side is weaker than unaffected side. Positive sign suggests tear in the supraspinatus.

recommended.name: Infraspinatus Test
recommended.procedure: Patient holds arms close to body, elbow is flexed up to 90 deg of forward elevation in scapular plane. External rotation is instructed while examiner applies resistance. Lack of power on one side indicates weakness of the infraspinatus muscle.

recommended.name: Subscapularis Test (Belly Press Test)
recommended.procedure: Patient is asked to place their hand on their abdomen and move elbow forward. Patient is then asked to press hand on the abdomen. If subscapularis is torn, patient will be unable to perform movement and elbow will move backwards.

recommended.name: Lag Sign for External Rotation
recommended.procedure: Patient lifts arm slightly from body and is asked to hold in external rotation. Positive when hand recoils to neutral position and suggests tear of infraspinatus or supraspinatus.

recommended.name: Drop Sign
recommended.procedure: The examiner places the arm at 90 deg abduction, elbow at right angle and arm maximally rotated. Positive sign: arm drops from position. Suggests a tear of the infraspinatus or the posterior part of the rotator cuff.

recommended.name: Lift-Off Test (Subscapularis)
recommended.procedure: Patient is asked to place hand on the back at the mid-lumbar spine. The clinician then lifts hand from the back and patient is asked to hold it there. Positive sign: inability to maintain hand while removed suggests subscapularis weakness.

recommended.name: Apprehension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient is in sitting or lying position, the examiner lifts the arm gently into abduction, external rotation and then extension. Test is positive if patient senses that humeral head is about to slip out anteriorly and body stiffens in apprehension. The test is repeated with the anterior part of shoulder protected.

recommended.name: Fulcrum's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine, arm abducted up to 90 deg. The examiner places their hands over the shoulder to set the fulcrum base. The humeral head is levered forward by extending and externally rotating arm. The patient immediately becomes apprehensive.

recommended.name: Drawer's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine, scapula is stabilised with one hand while the upper arm is grasped firmly with the other, and manoeuvring is done forward and backward (like a drawer). The drawer's test is positive if instability is marked.

recommended.procedure: Patient supine and relaxed. Examiner gently pushes the patella laterally. If positive, indicates patellar instability.

recommended.name: Patellar Tilt Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner lifts the lateral edge of the patella while stabilizing the medial edge. If positive, limited tilt or pain indicates tight lateral structures or OA changes.

recommended.name: Waldron Test
recommended.procedure: Patient seated and actively flexes and extends the knee while examiner palpates the patellofemoral joint. If positive, indicates PFPS or patellofemoral joint irritation.

recommended.name: Patellar Glide Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner glides the patella medially and laterally. If positive, indicates abnormal patellar tracking.

recommended.name: McMurray Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine. Examiner flexes the hip and knee fully, then rotates the tibia internally and externally while extending the knee. If positive, suggests meniscal tear.

recommended.name: Apley's Compression Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies prone with knee flexed to 90°. Examiner applies downward pressure along the tibia while rotating it internally and externally. If positive, indicates meniscal injury.

recommended.name: Thessaly Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands on one leg with knee slightly flexed (~20°). Patient rotates the body and knee internally and externally three times. If positive, indicates possible meniscal pathology.

recommended.name: Bounce Home Test
recommended.procedure: Patient supine. Examiner fully flexes the knee and then allows it to passively extend. If positive, suggests a displaced meniscal fragment.

recommended.name: Ege's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands with knees flexed and externally rotates both feet to test the medial meniscus; internally rotates both feet to test the lateral meniscus. If positive, pain or clicking occurs along the joint line.

recommended.name: Resisted Contraction Test
recommended.procedure: Patient contracts the affected muscle against resistance at mid-range. Positive if pain is reproduced at the site.

recommended.name: Passive Stretch Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner stretches the affected muscle slowly. Positive if pain is reproduced.

recommended.name: Lachman Test
recommended.procedure: Knee flexed ~30°, examiner stabilizes femur and pulls tibia anteriorly at the knee. Positive sign = soft endpoint or increased anterior tibial translation indicates ACL tear.

recommended.name: Anterior Drawer Test
recommended.procedure: Knee flexed 90°, examiner pulls tibia anteriorly at the knee. Positive sign = increased anterior translation indicates ACL injury.

recommended.name: Valgus Stress Test
recommended.procedure: With pt supine, knee flexed to 30°, examiner stabilizes the femur and applies a valgus force to the knee. Positive sign = pain or gapping at the medial knee joint line indicates MCL injury.

recommended.name: Varus Stress Test
recommended.procedure: With pt supine, knee flexed to 30°, examiner stabilizes the femur and applies a varus force to the knee. Positive sign = pain or gapping at the lateral knee joint line indicates LCL injury.

recommended.name: Posterior Drawer Test
recommended.procedure: Knee flexed 90°, examiner pushes tibia posteriorly at the knee. Positive sign = posterior translation indicates PCL tear.

recommended.name: Godfrey (Posterior Sag) Test
recommended.procedure: Hip and knee flexed 90°, examiner observes tibial plateau at the knee. Positive sign = sagging tibia compared to contralateral knee indicates PCL injury.

recommended.name: Patellofemoral Compression Test (Grind Test)
recommended.procedure: Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner applies downward pressure on the patella while asking the patient to contract the quadriceps. Positive sign = pain or crepitus at the patellofemoral joint.

recommended.name: Patellar Tilt Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner lifts the lateral edge of the patella while stabilizing the medial edge. Positive sign = limited tilt or pain indicates tight lateral structures or OA changes.

recommended.name: Crepitus Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner moves the knee through full flexion and extension, palpating and listening for audible or palpable crepitus.

recommended.name: Radiographic Confirmation
recommended.procedure: Check for joint space narrowing, osteophyte formation, subchondral sclerosis, and cyst formation

recommended.name: Patellar Apprehension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with the knee extended. Examiner gently pushes the patella laterally. Positive sign = apprehension or pain indicating abnormal patellar tracking.

recommended.name: Patellar Hyper-mobility Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine, knee extended. Examiner gently displaces patella medially and laterally. Positive sign = excessive hypermobility or abnormal motion.

recommended.name: Imaging
recommended.procedure: Lateral and axial X-rays; MRI if soft tissue assessment needed. Positive sign = subluxation/dislocation, osteochondral fractures, or MPFL tear.

recommended.name: Straight Leg Raise Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with both legs extended. Examiner asks the patient to lift the affected leg straight up without bending the knee. Positive sign = inability to lift the leg actively, indicating disruption of the extensor mechanism.

recommended.name: Palpation Test for Patella Integrity
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with knee relaxed. Examiner palpates the patella gently using fingers to feel for tenderness, irregularity, or gap. Positive sign = localized severe tenderness, palpable gap, or irregularity.

recommended.name: Active Knee Extension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient sits or lies supine. Examiner asks patient to actively straighten the knee from a flexed position. Positive sign = inability or severe pain during active extension.

recommended.name: Patellar Compression Test (Modified for fracture screening)
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with knee extended. Examiner gently presses patella posteriorly toward femur. Positive sign = severe localized pain, suggesting patella fracture.

recommended.name: Radiographic Confirmation
recommended.procedure: Imaging (X-ray – AP, Lateral, Skyline view). Positive sign = visible fracture line, displacement, or comminution.

recommended.name: Noble Compression Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine. Examiner flexes knee to 90° and applies pressure over lateral femoral epicondyle while slowly extending the knee. Positive sign = pain at approximately 30° knee flexion.

recommended.name: Ober's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies on unaffected side. Examiner extends and abducts the hip, then slowly lowers the leg. Positive sign = leg remains elevated and does not drop.

recommended.name: Renne Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands and performs squat while examiner applies pressure over lateral femoral epicondyle. Positive sign = pain at approximately 30° knee flexion.

recommended.name: Modified Thomas Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine at edge of table. Examiner observes hip and thigh position. Positive sign = tight lateral thigh indicating IT band tightness.

recommended.name: Palpation Test of Lateral Femoral Epicondyle
recommended.procedure: Examiner palpates lateral femoral epicondyle with knee flexed and extended.

recommended.name: Decline Squat Test
recommended.procedure: Patient stands on 25° decline board and performs squat. Positive sign = localized pain at inferior pole of patella.

recommended.name: Resisted Knee Extension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient sits with knee flexed. Examiner resists knee extension. Positive sign = localized tendon pain.

recommended.name: Single-Leg Decline Squat Test
recommended.procedure: Patient performs single-leg squat on decline surface. Positive sign = reproduction of localized tendon pain.

recommended.name: Palpation Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner palpates inferior and superior poles of patella. Positive sign = localized tenderness at tendon insertion.

recommended.name: Hop Test
recommended.procedure: Patient performs repeated hopping on affected leg. Positive sign = localized tendon pain with loading.

recommended.name: Pes Anserinus Palpation Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine with knee extended. Examiner palpates 5–7 cm below medial joint line. Positive sign = localized tenderness.

recommended.name: Resisted Knee Flexion Test
recommended.procedure: Patient flexes knee while examiner applies resistance. Positive sign = pain at pes anserinus region.

recommended.name: Resisted Hip Adduction Test
recommended.procedure: Patient performs hip adduction while examiner applies resistance. Positive sign = pain at pes anserinus insertion.

recommended.name: Hamstring Stretch Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner passively stretches hamstrings. Positive sign = pain at pes anserinus region.

recommended.name: Wilson's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine. Examiner flexes knee to 90°. Patient actively extends knee while examiner internally rotates tibia. Positive sign = pain between 30°–40° knee extension relieved with external rotation.

recommended.name: Passive Condylar Palpation Test
recommended.procedure: Patient knee flexed to 90°. Examiner palpates femoral condyles. Positive sign = localized pain over femoral condyle.

recommended.name: Joint Effusion Test (Stroke Test)
recommended.procedure: Examiner strokes medial knee upward and lateral knee downward. Positive sign = fluid movement or bulge.

recommended.name: Foucher's Sign
recommended.procedure: Positive sign = mass becomes firm in extension and softens or disappears in flexion, confirming Baker's cyst.

recommended.name: Popliteal Palpation Test
recommended.procedure: Patient prone or supine. Examiner palpates popliteal fossa. Positive sign = palpable fluid-filled mass.

recommended.name: Transillumination Test
recommended.procedure: Light source applied behind swelling. Positive sign = transillumination suggests fluid-filled cyst.

recommended.name: Knee Effusion Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner performs stroke test or bulge test. Positive sign = fluid accumulation present.

recommended.name: Lasègue's Test (Straight-Leg Raise)
recommended.procedure: Examiner raises legs of patient up so that hip flexion is achieved while knee is extended. Test is positive if patient feels pain along the course of the sciatic nerve and below the knee when hip is between 30-70 degrees of flexion.

recommended.name: Bragard Test
recommended.procedure: This is a modification of the SLR and dorsiflexion is applied at the end of the SLR. This reduces the angle where the test is positive.

recommended.name: Lasègue's Test (Straight-Leg Raise)
recommended.procedure: Examiner raises legs of patient up so that hip flexion is achieved while knee is extended. Test is positive if patient feels pain along the course of the sciatic nerve and below the knee when hip is between 30-70 degrees of flexion.

recommended.name: Bragard Test
recommended.procedure: This is a modification of the SLR and dorsiflexion is applied at the end of the SLR. This reduces the angle where the test is positive.

recommended.name: Bowstring Test (Popliteal Compression Test / Tibial Nerve Stretch Sign)
recommended.procedure: This can be done while patient is lying in supine or sitting position. The examiner flexes the knee and applies pressure on the popliteal fossa evoking sciatica.

recommended.name: Clinical Observation - Knee Jerk Reflex
recommended.procedure: Check if knee jerk reflex is present

recommended.name: Clinical Observation - Ankle Jerk Reflex
recommended.procedure: Check if ankle jerk reflex is present

recommended.name: Bicycle Stress Test
recommended.procedure: Record the amount of time the patient spends on a cycle ergometer while in a neutral lumbar position and slumped position. If patient spends more time in the slumped position, a lumbar spinal stenosis is indicated.

recommended.name: Two-stage Treadmill Test
recommended.procedure: The patient walks on a flat treadmill and the amount of time spent is recorded and compared with the amount of time while the treadmill is inclined such that patient walks in flexion.

recommended.name: Lumbar Extension-Loading Test
recommended.procedure: The examiner ensures that the lumbar region is in moderate extension (10-30 deg) while standing and patient lies supine. Check if there are changes in the symptoms that the patient feels.

recommended.name: Clinical Observation - Wide-based Gait
recommended.procedure: Check if a wide-based gait is present

recommended.name: Clinical Observation - Trendelenburg's Sign
recommended.procedure: Check if Trendelenburg's sign is present

recommended.name: Clinical Observation - Romberg Test
recommended.procedure: Check for negative Romberg test

recommended.name: Clinical Observation - Achilles Reflex
recommended.procedure: Check if Achilles tendon reflex is diminished

recommended.name: Lasègue's Test (Straight-Leg Raise)
recommended.procedure: Examiner raises legs of patient up so that hip flexion is achieved while knee is extended. Test is positive if patient feels pain along the course of the sciatic nerve and below the knee when hip is between 30-70 degrees of flexion.

recommended.name: Bragard Test
recommended.procedure: This is a modification of the SLR and dorsiflexion is applied at the end of the SLR. This reduces the angle where the test is positive.

recommended.name: Bowstring Test (Popliteal Compression Test / Tibial Nerve Stretch Sign)
recommended.procedure: This can be done while patient is lying in supine or sitting position. The examiner flexes the knee and applies pressure on the popliteal fossa evoking sciatica.

recommended.name: Femoral Nerve Stretch Test (Wasserman Sign)
recommended.procedure: Patient is in prone position, knee is flexed and hip is extended. Reproduction of pain in anterior thigh is positive.

recommended.name: Kernig Test
recommended.procedure: Patient's neck is flexed, hip flexed and the leg is extended. Pain is reproduced in this position.

recommended.name: Milgram Test
recommended.procedure: Pain is reproduced on straight leg elevation for 30 seconds.

recommended.name: MRI
recommended.procedure: Radiographic confirmation of disc herniation

recommended.name: Clinical Observation - Paraspinal Tenderness
recommended.procedure: Check for tenderness in the paraspinal musculature

recommended.name: Clinical Observation - Paraspinal Spasms
recommended.procedure: Check for spasms in the paraspinal musculature

recommended.name: Clinical Observation - Decreased Reflexes
recommended.procedure: Check for decreased reflexes: patellar and ankle jerk

recommended.name: Clinical Observation - Trendelenburg's Sign
recommended.procedure: Check for Trendelenburg's sign

recommended.name: MRI
recommended.procedure: Radiographic confirmation - urgent imaging required

recommended.name: Clinical Observation - Upper Motor Neuron Signs
recommended.procedure: Check for Babinski sign and clonus to rule out upper motor neuron involvement

recommended.name: Lateral Lumbar Flexion (Fingertip to Floor Test)
recommended.procedure: The patient stands with heel touching wall and feet wide apart, and back against the wall. Then the examiner measures the distance from middle finger to the floor. Then patient bends to side (lateral flexion). The distance between the middle finger and the floor is measured again. This measurement is done for both sides.

recommended.name: Modified Schober's Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner marks both posterior superior iliac spine, and a horizontal line is drawn between both marks. A second line is marked 5cm below the first line, and a third line is marked 10cm above the first line. Patient is then instructed to flex forward as if attempting to touch their toes. An increase of less than 5cm shows decreased lumbar spine range of motion, and ankylosing spondylitis.

recommended.name: Chest Expansion Test
recommended.procedure: Normal chest expansion is ≥ 5 cm

recommended.name: Occiput to Wall Distance
recommended.procedure: Normal distance is 0

recommended.name: Tragus to Wall Distance
recommended.procedure: Normal distance is < 15cm

recommended.name: Intermalleolar Distance
recommended.procedure: Normal distance is > 100cm

recommended.name: Laboratory Investigations
recommended.procedure: Confirmatory test through laboratory investigations (HLA-B27, ESR, CRP)

recommended.name: Radiographic Confirmation
recommended.procedure: X-ray to check for fracture location and displacement

recommended.name: Spurling's Test (for Cervical Radiculitis)
recommended.procedure: While patient is seated, the examiner applies side flexion of the neck towards the affected side while applying axial compression. Sign is positive if the pain sensation felt in the shoulder-neck region is replicated.

recommended.name: Painful Arc Test
recommended.procedure: Ask patient to abduct arm across range of motion actively. Scapular rhythm is disturbed, pain is aggravated between 60-120 degrees, pain is alleviated if shoulder is laterally rotated on abduction. If positive, SIS is indicated.

recommended.name: Neer Impingement Sign
recommended.procedure: Stabilise the scapula with one hand and raise the unaffected side to full flexion with abduction and internal rotation passively. The test is positive when there is pain at the subacromial space.

recommended.name: Hawkins-Kennedy Test
recommended.procedure: Patient arm is placed in 90 deg of elevation at the scapular level and 90 deg flexion. Stabilise the upper arm with one hand and internally rotate with the other hand. The test is positive when pain is felt in the anterolateral aspect of the shoulder.

recommended.name: Jobe's Test
recommended.procedure: Elevate arm in scapular plane, extend elbow and thumb points towards floor with arm internally rotated. Patient is asked to hold the position with downward pressure from examiner. Positive sign = pain on examiner restriction indicating supraspinatus irritation.

recommended.name: Clinical Assessment
recommended.procedure: Physical examination and clinical assessment based on presenting symptoms

recommended.name: Clinical Observation - Bicipital Groove
recommended.procedure: Check for tenderness along the bicipital groove or on moving the biceps tendon (bicipital tendinitis can co-exist with other rotator cuff pathologies)

recommended.name: Empty Can Test (Supraspinatus)
recommended.procedure: Patient is asked to abduct up to 90 deg, 30 deg flexion and internal rotation. Examiner stands behind patient and applies downward pressure. Positive sign: affected side is weaker than unaffected side. Positive sign suggests tear in the supraspinatus.

recommended.name: Infraspinatus Test
recommended.procedure: Patient holds arms close to body, elbow is flexed up to 90 deg of forward elevation in scapular plane. External rotation is instructed while examiner applies resistance. Lack of power on one side indicates weakness of the infraspinatus muscle.

recommended.name: Subscapularis Test (Belly Press Test)
recommended.procedure: Patient is asked to place their hand on their abdomen and move elbow forward. Patient is then asked to press hand on the abdomen. If subscapularis is torn, patient will be unable to perform movement and elbow will move backwards.

recommended.name: Lag Sign for External Rotation
recommended.procedure: Patient lifts arm slightly from body and is asked to hold in external rotation. Positive when hand recoils to neutral position and suggests tear of infraspinatus or supraspinatus.

recommended.name: Drop Sign
recommended.procedure: The examiner places the arm at 90 deg abduction, elbow at right angle and arm maximally rotated. Positive sign: arm drops from position. Suggests a tear of the infraspinatus or the posterior part of the rotator cuff.

recommended.name: Lift-Off Test (Subscapularis)
recommended.procedure: Patient is asked to place hand on the back at the mid-lumbar spine. The clinician then lifts hand from the back and patient is asked to hold it there. Positive sign: inability to maintain hand while removed suggests subscapularis weakness.

recommended.name: X-ray
recommended.procedure: Check X-ray to rule out asymptomatic calcification

recommended.name: Apprehension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient is in sitting or lying position, the examiner lifts the arm gently into abduction, external rotation and then extension. Test is positive if patient senses that humeral head is about to slip out anteriorly and body stiffens in apprehension. The test is repeated with the anterior part of shoulder protected.

recommended.name: Fulcrum's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine, arm abducted up to 90 deg. The examiner places their hands over the shoulder to set the fulcrum base. The humeral head is levered forward by extending and externally rotating arm. The patient immediately becomes apprehensive.

recommended.name: Drawer's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient lies supine, scapula is stabilised with one hand while the upper arm is grasped firmly with the other, and manoeuvring is done forward and backward (like a drawer). The drawer's test is positive if instability is marked.

recommended.name: Radiographic Confirmation
recommended.procedure: Check for periarticular erosions, subchondral sclerosis, and resorption

recommended.name: Radiographic Confirmation
recommended.procedure: Check for distortion of the joint, subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte formation, and narrowing of articular space

recommended.name: Clinical Assessment
recommended.procedure: Physical examination and clinical assessment based on presenting symptoms

recommended.name: Phalen's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient flexes wrists fully and holds position. If positive, indicates CTS.

recommended.name: Tinel's Sign
recommended.procedure: Examiner taps over carpal tunnel. If positive, indicates CTS.

recommended.name: Carpal Compression Test
recommended.procedure: Examiner applies direct pressure over carpal tunnel. If positive, indicates CTS.

recommended.name: Finkelstein's Test
recommended.procedure: Patient makes a fist with thumb inside fingers. Examiner ulnar deviates wrist. If positive, indicates De Quervain's.

recommended.name: WHAT Test (Wrist Hyperflexion Abduction of Thumb)
recommended.procedure: Patient hyperflexes wrist and abducts thumb against resistance. If positive, indicates De Quervain's.

recommended.name: Ligament Stress Tests
recommended.procedure: Examiner applies stress to specific ligaments. Positive sign = pain or instability localized to the injured ligament.

recommended.name: Radiographic Confirmation
recommended.procedure: Rule out undisplaced fracture or other bony injury

recommended.name: TFCC Load Test
recommended.procedure: Wrist in ulnar deviation + axial load + rotation. Positive if ulnar wrist pain.

recommended.name: Press Test
recommended.procedure: Patient pushes up from chair using hands. Positive if ulnar wrist pain.

recommended.name: Radiographic Confirmation
recommended.procedure: MRI or arthrogram to assess TFCC complex integrity

recommended.name: Transillumination Test
recommended.procedure: Light is applied through the swelling. Positive sign = transillumination confirms fluid-filled cyst.

recommended.name: Resisted Wrist Extension Test
recommended.procedure: Patient extends wrist against resistance. Positive sign = pain 4–6 cm proximal to the wrist in the dorsal radial forearm.

recommended.name: Snuffbox Tenderness Test
recommended.procedure: Palpation of anatomical snuffbox. If positive, indicates scaphoid fracture.

recommended.name: Scaphoid Compression Test
recommended.procedure: Axial load applied through thumb. If positive, indicates scaphoid fracture.

recommended.name: Radiographic Confirmation
recommended.procedure: X-ray and/or MRI to confirm scaphoid fracture, especially if initial X-ray is normal.

recommended.name: Axial Load Test
recommended.procedure: Apply compression through wrist. Positive if central dorsal wrist pain.

recommended.name: Radiographic Confirmation
recommended.procedure: X-ray for staging, MRI for early AVN detection.
